name: Monodiplos

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Monodiplos originates from the Messenia region in the Peloponnese.
It was formally documented in the 2009 research 'Horoi apo Messiniaki Gis' by Evangelos Lambpropoulos.
on_screen: Map: Greece · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: A social dance used for celebrations and community gatherings, emphasizing the rhythmic transition between single and double steps.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is a variation of the Kalamatiano.
It features a specific sequence of a single step followed by a double step back variation.
Watch for Double step back.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circular progression moving to the right
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is typically performed to the song 'Stin Apano Geitonia'.
It follows the 7/8 rhythm characteristic of the Kalamatiano.
Listen for the Clarinet, Violin, Lute, Santouri.
The pulse is 7/8 at about 130 beats a minute.
A bright, driving 7/8 rhythm led by a melodic clarinet, featuring the specific 'Stin Apano Geitonia' melody which dictates the step changes.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Stin Apano Geitonia — Traditional
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Long-short-short (3+2+2)

scenes.title: The costume and the setting

scenes.title: The people
narration: Evangelos Lambpropoulos is the primary researcher who documented the dance in 2009.
While a form of Kalamatiano, the Monodiplos is specific to the Messenian land.
It is a subclass of Greek folk dance and a direct variant of the Kalamatiano/Syrtos family.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Monodiplos is parent of Kalamatiano: Monodiplos is a specific variation of the Kalamatiano dance.
Monodiplos is sibling of Syrtos: Both belong to the broader family of Greek dragging dances.

music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.sound_description: A bright, driving 7/8 rhythm led by a melodic clarinet, featuring the specific 'Stin Apano Geitonia' melody which dictates the step changes.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Monodiplos (Greece). Meter 7/8. Tempo about 130 bpm. Rhythm pattern: Long-short-short (3+2+2). Instruments: Clarinet, Violin, Lute, Santouri. Vocal style: Greek folk (Dimotiko). Form: Strophic with instrumental interludes. Mood: festive, rhythmic, communal. It should sound like this: A bright, driving 7/8 rhythm led by a melodic clarinet, featuring the specific 'Stin Apano Geitonia' melody which dictates the step changes. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
